title: US Tightens AI Chip Exports, Jane Street's Anthropic Windfall | OWITH Daily
description:
The Commerce Department requires licenses for AI chip exports to data centers in Singapore, Malaysia and three other countries, and Jane Street's FTX purchase of Anthropic shares could be worth over thirty five billion dollars at the IPO. Also: Goldman Sachs says the AI layoff wave is delayed, Wharton and Accenture on what agentic AI really costs, Verizon's AI plan for customer service, and Monday's bank outages.

Good morning from OWITH.ai, the briefing that gives you only what's important to hear in AI and tech. It's Tuesday, November 17.

Today, Washington tightens the rules on AI chips flowing through Southeast Asia, and a trading firm stands to make a fortune from Anthropic's stock market debut.

We start with the Commerce Department. Fortune reports that its Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule on Monday requiring licenses to export advanced AI chips to data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Large data center operators anywhere in the world now also need a license to give companies headquartered in China access to those chips, and operators already serving such clients have ninety days to get one. Companies owned by American firms, such as Microsoft, Oracle and Amazon, get a carve out. The rule closes a loophole that let Chinese companies use controlled chips in overseas data centers, and anyone building or renting compute in Southeast Asia now faces a licensing review.

Next, the Anthropic listing is days away, and one early winner is easy to spot. Fortune reports that Jane Street paid one point three four billion dollars in 2024 for the Anthropic shares that FTX's bankruptcy administrators sold to repay customers. At a proposed range of seventy to seventy eight dollars a share, valuing Anthropic at up to roughly one point four trillion dollars, that stake could be worth more than thirty five billion. A vehicle linked to Abu Dhabi's Mubadala and the Ford Foundation also bought shares. Pricing is expected on Wednesday, with Nasdaq trading on Thursday. The gap between what early holders paid and what public investors will pay shows how much of the AI boom has already been captured privately.

On jobs, Fortune reports that Goldman Sachs' outlook for 2027, published Sunday night, describes a labor market where companies neither hire nor fire much, and expects that to last about one more year. Goldman forecasts growth of two point four percent next year and no recession. Its economists expect AI related job losses to grow later, mostly during a downturn. Goldman economist Joseph Briggs estimated last month that up to nine percent of workers could be displaced during the transition, and wrote that automation disruption tends to accelerate in slowdowns. For leaders, the quiet so far says little about what happens when the cycle turns.

A new report from the Wharton School and Accenture asks what agentic AI really costs. The authors studied more than eighteen thousand tasks across nine hundred and twenty three occupations. Of the roughly eleven thousand tasks AI agents could take on, more than ninety percent are routine enough for cheaper models. In each of the nineteen industries studied, only six to eleven percent of agent work needs a frontier model. That matters because total AI bills keep rising even as the cost per task falls, since companies hand more work to agents. For a firm with one hundred thousand employees running thirty five agents, five year costs range from about one hundred fifty five million dollars in health care to five hundred twenty million in insurance.

In an interview with Fortune, Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said most of the company's customer service is outsourced, mainly to the Philippines, and that a lot of it will be automated. AI agents already handle routine requests like password resets and roaming setup, drawing on about three hundred data points per customer. The most complex calls, which he says are hard to automate, are likely to be brought back to the United States. This is a concrete template for how AI reshapes a service workforce. Offshore volume shrinks first, and the human work that remains moves closer to home and up in difficulty.

Customers of several large American banks had trouble on Monday. Fortune reports that Downdetector complaints about Chase passed twenty thousand by early afternoon Eastern time, covering app logins, money transfers, ATMs and Zelle. Bank of America, Wells Fargo and U.S. Bank each drew between one and two thousand reports. Chase blamed a technical issue and said customers could still access their accounts, and Wells Fargo said it was fixing a technical issue. It was unclear whether the problems shared a cause. Coming days after the Microsoft email outage and the FAA ground stop, it is another prompt for boards to test their own resilience plans.

The thread today is that AI's real costs and risks are moving out of the lab and into the plumbing: chip licenses, cloud bills, call centers and the systems everyone assumes will simply work.

That's it for today. Thanks for listening to OWITH.ai. See you tomorrow.
